rmk: This clip offers a comparison between BLACKCAP and then GARDEN WARBLER (from 0:40). Both were singing in the same area. The Blackcap recording features two males that were 'song sparring' but, somewhat unfortunately, the Garden Warbler clip has a WILLOW WARBLER overlapping at 0:47 and then a CHAFFINCH at 0:51. The chief means for distinguishing between the Blackcap and Garden Warbler could be summarised as, for BLACKCAP, a more explosive song burst with 'spiky'  (heterogeneous) notes that, in these typical short bursts used by males when singing against each other, usually have a well defined finale.  GARDEN WARBLER has, if anything, a faster rate of singing but it sounds softer and more purring without a well-defined finale. Although Garden Warbler sings at a rapid pace, the pitch is slightly lower and the sound is more steady (homogeneous) than a Blackcap. The quality of Garden Warbler sound is hard to describe but it could be said to be a fast puttering?

rmk: This clip offers a comparison between BLACKCAP and then GARDEN WARBLER (from 0:40). Both were singing in the same area. The Blackcap recording features two males that were 'song sparring' but, somewhat unfortunately, the Garden Warbler clip has a WILLOW WARBLER overlapping at 0:47 and then a CHAFFINCH at 0:51. The chief means for distinguishing between the Blackcap and Garden Warbler could be summarised as, for BLACKCAP, a more explosive song burst with 'spiky' (heterogeneous) notes that, in these typical short bursts used by males when singing against each other, usually have a well defined finale. GARDEN WARBLER has, if anything, a faster rate of singing but it sounds softer and more purring without a well-defined finale. Although Garden Warbler sings at a rapid pace - even slightly faster than Blackcap - the pitch is lower, the sound is more steady (homogeneous) than a Blackcap, and the the ending fizzles out rather than ends with an emphasised note.

rmk: I accompanied this male for about an hour and a half as he sang throughout his territory while feeding occasionally. He moved around in an area of approximately 100 square metres on the riverbank, which consisted of riverside woodland (mainly willows and ash trees), a stone wall separating the river from the adjacent fields, dense low vegetation, and two or three wild rose bushes. It was “patrolling” the territory from one end to the other, and every time it heard another male singing in the distance, it would climb to the top of a bush (mainly a rose bush) and sing. There were times when, climbing up from the vegetation, he would perch less than two metres away from me and the parabola to sing. On two occasions, another bird passed through the low vegetation without vocalising (a female?), and this male interacted with another supposed male at one end of the territory. In this recording, he sings for 20 seconds without practically stopping!

type: flight call, Social calls, wing beats
rmk: Long-term recording of two pairs of birds in pursuit flights and interacting vocally. Four birds were observed, grouped in twos, which for 5-6 minutes were doing chase flights, falling flights typical of the species and vocalising. The question remains as to whether it was two pairs in territorial pursuit, although it seems to me that they were being that aggressive, or two adults with the two juveniles from the previous year training for display flights. In the recording we hear three types of interaction calls, the most characteristic "krrah", an "ohh" and a prolonged "róóóó". The beating of the wings is also heard several times.
